answer:
Under the Universal Scalability Law, relative capacity is C(N) = N / [1 + α(N−1) + βN(N−1)]. The numerator rises linearly with N, but the denominator contains a βN(N−1) coherency term that rises roughly quadratically. Once coordination work — shared locks, cache invalidation, cross-worker messaging — grows faster than the useful work each new worker adds, aggregate throughput peaks and then turns retrograde. Contention alone produces diminishing returns; positive β is what can make extra workers counterproductive.

The fitted α and β cannot identify the cause. They are aggregate empirical parameters for contention and coherence, and the expression is not a mechanism detector: a particular lock, link or invalidation flow cannot be proven from the coefficients. Different mechanisms can produce similar curves, especially when the fit spans few points, a changing workload mix or confounded resource limits; warm-up, retries and generator limits add further ambiguity. Fitted coefficients support prediction inside the observed envelope, not causal diagnosis.

Distinguishing causes requires controlled experiments: hold fixture, skew, versions and backend ceiling fixed, vary replicas, then inspect lock wait/hold time, per-key contention, pool acquisition, invalidation work and queue age. Confidence is conceptual: the source ledger records no fitted Tycho curve or benchmark.

Evidence map: workload-shape-and-scalability-laws §3; scaling-models §3; measurement-model; contention-response §§5–6.

evidence.claim: USL normalizes relative capacity as C(N)=N/[1+α(N−1)+βN(N−1)], with α contention and β coherency overhead; fit comparable measured points because the equation is not proof of a particular bottleneck.
evidence.note: Observed in section text. The linear-vs-quadratic explanation of the peak is my derivation from the stated formula (inference).

evidence.claim: The curve shows diminishing returns when shared-resource contention dominates and retrograde throughput at higher N when coordination work increases faster than useful work.
evidence.note: Observed bullets in the canonical scaling-models section.

evidence.claim: α and β are empirical fitting parameters; the expression is not a mechanism detector, and fitted coefficients cannot prove that a particular lock, network link or cache-invalidation flow is the cause.
evidence.note: Observed, nearly verbatim; the key boundary for the second half of the question.

evidence.claim: A fit needs enough observations with the same workload mix and bounded resource costs; compare withheld test points, retain uncertainty and investigate bottleneck signals rather than trusting a pretty sparse curve.
evidence.note: Observed guidance in the same section.

evidence.claim: The USL is a model fitted against observations, not a law that identifies contention or coherence costs from a single data point; fitting coefficients to too few samples is not mechanism evidence.

Discriminating mechanisms requires freezing fixture, skew, versions and dependency limits, varying replicas at a constant backend ceiling, observing bottleneck shifts, and fitting only after enough stable comparable observations.
